<reason>Both sides fought a genuinely sharp, narrow clash. CON's best work was original and well-executed: the "genuinely necessary is unidentifiable in advance" attack, the vacuum argument (weight redistributing to referrals, employer prestige, and the interview), the Griggs-style causal story for why the degree became the defensible proxy, and the licensing/cheap-error distinction that answered PRO's cashier/driver/electrician pressure question crisply. Its closing gotcha — "complied, if the review was honest" — was the sharpest single moment of the debate. But PRO neutralized the two loads CON needed. First, the equity turn: "polish contests happen in both worlds; the degree simply removes the poor candidate before he reaches one," plus the observation that referrals and interviews already sit on top of the filter today, so removing the credential adds a hearing rather than summoning new bias. CON's reply that the diploma is the one asset a networkless stranger can earn alone was directly punctured by PRO's point that it cannot be earned without money or debt; "a scholarship exists" is a thinner answer than the objection deserved. Second, the dilemma: PRO's framing of the motion as a standard of practice, analogous to "don't ask applicants their age," is a plausible answer that CON's demand for a tribunal and pre-hire evidence partly evades by replacing the proposition with an enforceability question. PRO also kept the affirmative weighing alive — a filter that discards most adults, tracks parental wealth, was never validated, and has cheaper direct substitutes — and correctly flagged that CON offered risk-of-substitution but never weighed the scale of the exclusion. CON's natural-experiment argument was fought to roughly a draw, with PRO's "firms changed the wording, not the screening; the motion targets screening" the marginally better resolution. Both sides labeled Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 properly; PRO paid a real execution cost for three clipped turns, including a truncated final weighing, which keeps the margin competitive rather than solid.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's answer to the vacuum/equity argument: graduates get interviewed too, so the interview is a constant in both worlds, and the degree merely eliminates the poor candidate before gate one — combined with the closing puncture of CON's "credential a networkless stranger can acquire alone," which cannot be acquired without money or debt. That exchange gutted CON's strongest comparative claim that removing the filter makes hiring more wealth-wired.</best_rebuttal>
